texts: bad: "iron-lidded" has to stay one unanalyzed property of the bin, so the lid it names stays unreachable; this parse instead invented a lid the sentence never introduces and predicated "iron" of it, which is not licensed, and left the bin with no iron-lidded property at all. If the lid matters, give it a noun phrase of its own: "The feather bin is a box in the floor of the ledger-room, and the bin has an iron lid."
good. the bin, the holding, the large reserve and the feathers it consists of are all covered.

bad: "keys" comes out as one single set shared by everyone -- every council member and Tessa Brae are recorded as holding the very same keys, which the sentence does not say. Rewrite so each holder's key is introduced separately: "Each council member holds a key to the feather bin, and Tessa Brae holds a key to the feather bin." (The "key to X" link itself is on unsettled ground in the instruction set, so expect it to be recorded loosely either way.)
good. the named hall, the salt-bloom store, its link to the hall and its wooden-cabinet kind are all carried.

good. it becomes a fireable per-compartment rule with its own harvest for each compartment; the word "one" is not separately recorded, but the rule already says exactly one harvest per compartment, so nothing is lost.
good. the two verbs each get their own per-harvest rule with Hesper as the doer, so "dates" and "labels" are both covered.

bad: "within a season" has nothing to attach to, so the parse states the old-before-new ordering with no time limit at all -- a stronger claim than you made -- and the only alternative available is to drop the ordering entirely, which loses the point of the sentence. Rewrite with "during" and two full clauses: "During each season, keepers use old salt-bloom before they use new salt-bloom." -- "during" gives the season something concrete to hold both usings inside, and spelling out the second clause keeps the two usings distinguishable.
